newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Arresting suspects not NATO's job -- U.S. general.
newsitem.headline: Arresting suspects not NATO's job -- U.S. general.

text.p: U.S. General John Shalikashvili on Monday called for a special police force to be set up to arrest war crimes suspects in Bosnia, saying it was not a job for the NATO-led peace force.
The chairman of the U.S. joint chiefs of staff told reporters during a visit to Sarajevo that NATO's new 18-month peacekeeping mission did not call for its troops to arrest war crimes suspects.
But he said a separate police force should be formed to go after indicted war criminals who have not been handed over as required by the Dayton peace accords.

"I think a way must be found where a police force can be constituted that would take care in those instances where the signatories to the (agreement) continue to refuse to turn over those war criminals," Shalikashvili said.
He made clear NATO would not contribute to such a police force. "I think NATO should in my judgment confine itself to the military aspects of this operation. They've done that job extremely well."
The U.S. general's comments appeared aimed at deflecting calls for NATO to take action against indicted war criminals.
The international High Representative to Bosnia, Carl Bildt, has called on Western powers to form a specially trained unit that would apprehend those charged with war crimes.
Most of those indicted by the U.N. war crimes tribunal in the Hague remain at large one year since Bosnia's rival factions signed the peace treaty.
The two most prominent suspects, wartime Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and retired Serb army commander Ratko Mladic, continue to exert influence in Bosnia's Serb republic.
NATO commanders, fearing possible casualties and a backlash against their troops, have ruled out "manhunts" and say their troops will arrest suspects only if they encounter them during their duties.
Balkan commentators have criticised the NATO alliance's stance and say that no lasting peace can be built in former Yugoslavia if indicted war criminals are allowed to go free.
Shalikashvili said that NATO troops were not qualified for what he called "police work".

"I must tell you after many years of experience I am convinced that we must not make the mistake to think that soldiers, because they do soldierly acts well, are also trained policemen and can do police work well."
A civilian International Police Task Force (IPTF) already operates in Bosnia, but it is only mandated to observe and assist local police and has not been directly involved in arrests.
Shalikashvili flew to Bosnia four days before the formal launching of a new peacekeeping mission which succeeds the NATO-led implementation force (IFOR).
The new stabilisation force (SFOR) will enforce Bosnia's peace treaty with some 30,000 troops, including 8,500 American soldiers.
IFOR had close to 60,000 troops at its height but has gradually reduced its strength over the past several months.
Under the comand of U.S. General William Crouch, SFOR will include 3,000 German combat troops -- the first to serve abroad since World War Two.
Shalikashvili said NATO believed it could fulfil peacekeeping goals within the 18-month mandate, but said the misson's status would be reviewed every six months.
"It is our hope now that in 18 months the operation can be terminated and everyone can go home," he said.
